Gynecology and urology · published research

Testicle function

Several testicular-injury models reported improved sperm or tissue measures, while other experiments found dose-related harm or no significant hormone change. A recent busulfan mouse study reported only nonsignificant in-vivo trends. A mapped spinal-cord injury model also reported better testicular outcomes after PBM was directed at the injured cord. The only human report was an uncontrolled series with increased sperm counts in some men; clinical fertility benefit has not been established.

Publications and records

19relevant publications

Publication and study types

Animal: 18 (mouse; rat; ram)

Human case series: 1 (20 men, mapped from male infertility)

No clinical trial

Separate ejaculated-sperm studies are not counted as testicle treatment studies

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Human case series (n=20; uncontrolled): among 16 men with oligospermia, reported sperm counts rose 2–5-fold; 4 men with azoospermia showed no improvement. No comparator or conception/live-birth outcomes were reported, so this is not a causal fertility-success estimate (Hasan et al., 1989).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for selected sperm and tissue outcomes in injury models

Very low for fertility outcomes in people

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several testicular-injury models reported improved sperm or tissue measures, while other experiments found dose-related harm or no significant hormone change. A recent busulfan mouse study reported only nonsignificant in-vivo trends. A mapped spinal-cord injury model also reported better testicular outcomes after PBM was directed at the injured cord. The only human report was an uncontrolled series with increased sperm counts in some men; clinical fertility benefit has not been established.

Summary of the Evidence

Nineteen relevant publications were identified after separating direct from mapped evidence: eight animal studies focused on testicular or testicle-function outcomes, nine animal studies mapped from related testicular-injury, sperm, or infertility categories, one additional rat spinal-cord injury experiment measured testicular function after PBM was directed at the injured cord, and one human case series was mapped from male infertility. The animal studies use distinct injury models rather than repeating one cohort. A broader literature irradiates ejaculated sperm outside the body; those experiments address laboratory sperm handling and are not included in this total.

Human and clinical evidence

The only human report was a 1989 uncontrolled case series of 20 men with infertility. None of four men with azoospermia showed improvement. Among 16 men with oligospermia, reported sperm counts increased two- to five-fold; several men had fewer abnormal sperm, and 15 reported increased libido. There was no comparison group and no report of conception or live birth, so these observations cannot establish a treatment effect on fertility (Hasan et al., 1989).

Animal evidence

Across mouse and rat models of scrotal heat, torsion, diabetes, toxic injury, and busulfan-induced azoospermia, PBM often increased sperm count, motility, viability, testicular cell measures, or antioxidant markers and reduced oxidative stress or tissue damage. A 2025 mouse study compared PBM after prolonged scrotal heat or busulfan and reported higher testicular-cell measures, sperm parameters, and testosterone in the busulfan-plus-PBM group than in the heat-plus-PBM group (Aqajanpor et al., 2025). A mouse heat-injury study reported improved sperm parameters and testicular histology after near-infrared exposure (Aghajanpour et al., 2024). A torsion model likewise reported better sperm quality, seminiferous structure, and antioxidant status (Afshar et al., 2026).

A separate rat spinal-cord-contusion experiment measured reproductive outcomes after applying PBM to the injured spinal-cord region rather than directly to the testes. Compared with untreated injury, the PBM group had higher sperm count, motility, viability, and testosterone, lower inflammatory markers, and less testicular cell loss. This is mapped evidence for secondary testicular dysfunction after spinal injury, not a direct testicular-treatment experiment (Taheri et al., 2025).

The direction was not uniformly favorable. In a ram degeneration model, 808-nm treatment at 28 J/cm² was associated with semen injury. Rat experiments also reported lower luteinizing hormone at a higher exposure, no significant overall testosterone rise, and seminiferous-tissue damage at the higher of two tested doses. A rat inflammation comparison found lower C-reactive protein with ultrasound than with laser, so PBM did not outperform the comparator in that outcome. A 2026 busulfan mouse experiment reported directional in-vivo increases in VASA expression, germ-cell activity, and sperm production, but those differences were not statistically significant (Tajalli et al., 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Many separate studies irradiate collected human or animal semen and measure motility, viability, or mitochondrial activity. These are ex-vivo or in-vitro sperm-cell experiments, not treatment of intact testes. A 2026 study also cultured spermatogonial stem cells from azoospermic mice and reported changes in several spermatogenesis-related genes after 808-nm irradiation at 4 J/cm²; this laboratory finding does not establish a fertility benefit in people (Tajalli et al., 2026).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Animal protocols ranged from red visible light around 660 nm to near-infrared wavelengths around 808–890 nm, with substantially different doses and schedules. The 2025 busulfan and heat model used laser irradiation reported as 0.03 J/cm²/sec every other day for 35 days. In the 2026 azoospermia study, the in-vivo protocol used 808 nm at 8 J/cm² and the stem-cell experiment used 4 J/cm². Several mouse injury studies used 890-nm near-infrared light at approximately 0.03 J/cm²; a rat spinal-cord-injury study used 810-nm near-infrared light at 150 mW for 50 minutes daily over two weeks, directed to the cord, and did not report fluence in the database. Other rat work compared 830-nm exposures of approximately 28 and 47 J/cm² and found tissue responses that differed by dose. The human case series combined 633-nm red He-Ne and pulsed 904-nm near-infrared light at 1.3 J/cm². These protocols do not define a transferable optimum.

Interpretation

Animal studies show improvements in sperm and tissue measures in several direct injury models, including a 2025 busulfan model, while a mapped spinal-cord experiment also found better testicular outcomes after cord-directed PBM. The newer 2026 in-vivo mouse study was not statistically significant, and other experiments identify dose-related harm and null hormone outcomes. The single human case series cannot determine whether the reported semen changes improve the chance of conception. Testicle-directed PBM therefore remains primarily a preclinical research topic.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Animal experiments repeatedly report better sperm, tissue, or hormone measures after heat, torsion, toxic, or diabetic injury, but some wavelengths and higher doses caused damage. The only mapped human report was an uncontrolled 20-man series from 1989. Even a recent busulfan mouse study reported only nonsignificant in-vivo trends. Independent clinical trials should track semen quality, hormones, conception, live birth, and delayed harms with a prespecified dose.
